hints: Focus on the shape of the graph, a gentle rise to a clear peak at R followed by a very sharp fall to S and T.
Recall that in Period 3 the metals Na, Mg and Al are good conductors, while Si and the non-metals after it conduct very poorly.
Check which element must sit at the peak for each property, for melting point the peak is Si but for conductivity the peak is Al, then match this to consecutive order.
walkthrough:
**Read the shape of graph X**

Look carefully at what the picture is telling you. P to Q rises a little, Q to R rises a lot to a maximum, then R to S falls sharply to a very low value that stays low to T.

So X is high for the first three elements and very low for the last two.

**Recall the Period 3 trends**

List Period 3 in order: $\text{Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar}$. Now think about each property.

Electrical conductivity: high for $\text{Na, Mg, Al}$, very low for $\text{Si, P, S, Cl, Ar}$, with $\text{Al}$ highest. Melting point: rises to a maximum at $\text{Si}$ then falls sharply. Electronegativity and ionisation energy: generally rise across the period with no sharp peak then collapse.

**Match the peak to element R**

Only a property that peaks at a metal and then collapses for the metalloid and non-metals fits. That is electrical conductivity.

If $\text{R} = \text{Al}$, then $\text{P} = \text{Na}$, $\text{Q} = \text{Mg}$, $\text{S} = \text{Si}$, $\text{T} = \text{P}$. This gives high, higher, highest, then a sharp drop to almost zero, exactly the graph shown.

options.A: Electrical conductivity is high for Na, slightly higher for Mg, highest for Al, then drops sharply to very low for Si and P. With P = Na, Q = Mg, R = Al, S = Si, T = P the graph shape is perfectly reproduced.
options.B: Electronegativity increases steadily across Period 3 from Na to Cl. It does not show a peak at the third element followed by a sharp collapse, so it cannot give the R peak and S, T low pattern.
options.C: Melting point does show a peak then a sharp fall, but the peak is at Si (giant covalent) not Al. If R were Al, the trend would still be rising to Si, so R = Al is wrong for this property. The trap is confusing the conductivity maximum (Al) with the melting point maximum (Si).
options.D: Second ionisation energy generally increases across the period with some irregularities, but it does not collapse after Si. For P = Mg, Q = Al, R = Si, S = P, T = S the values go up and down but stay high, with S and T higher than P. There is no sharp drop to near zero.
